rationale.conceptual: The underlying method—modal analysis of a piezoelectric structure in FEA—is an established technique, but implementing it correctly requires domain knowledge of piezoelectric coupling, material property assignment, and the effective coupling coefficient derivation. Multiple interacting components (geometry, meshing, solver settings, two electrical boundary conditions) must be coordinated, placing it above a simple textbook operation.
rationale.execution: The pipeline spans 4–5 stages: building two finite element models, running two modal analyses, extracting keff data, computing the coupling coefficient and spurious mode flags, and writing three output artifacts. Setting up the open‑source FEA tool, ensuring correct piezoelectric physics, and scripting the workflow adds moderate orchestration complexity.

difficulty.reasoning: The task requires setting up a 2D axisymmetric piezoelectric finite element model for two ring geometries, performing modal analysis, and extracting the effective electromechanical coupling coefficient versus frequency. The method is standard FEA but involves careful handling of piezoelectric material constants, boundary conditions, and the keff calculation from eigenfrequencies. The pipeline has multiple steps (model building, two simulations, post-processing, report generation) and depends on installing/configuring an open‑source FEA tool. Both the conceptual domain (piezoelectrics) and the engineering orchestration are non‑trivial but not research‑grade novel.

compute_estimate.reasoning: The paper’s 2D axisymmetric FEA ran on a Pentium IV with 256 MB RAM in minutes; a modern CPU with ~2 GB RAM easily handles the same modal analysis. No GPU is required, and the material data (Pz26 constants) is a few kilobytes.
